title: The Best Person I Ever Managed Almost Quit Because of Me
author: Kelly McGinnis
summary: McGinnis recounts the one-on-one in which one of her best employees told her she had no idea whether she was doing a good job, never got direction or time to think, and could see her manager favored a colleague. The colleague was wired like McGinnis, fast, instinctive and hungry for autonomy, which made leading him effortless and made her mistake the ease for skill. She had led the thorough, reflective employee the same way, putting her on the spot in meetings and never voicing the praise she privately felt, because she herself never needed reassurance. The repair turned out to be five plain questions about what the employee valued in a leader, how often to meet, how much direction and space she wanted, and how she wanted feedback. With structure, alignment up front and time to think, the employee stayed and became a strong leader. McGinnis draws two lessons: you cannot lead everyone the same way, and teams built in a leader's own image form a hall of mirrors that never makes anyone a better leader.
points: McGinnis realized that managing someone just like herself felt like competence but required no skill at all.
Because she never sought reassurance, she assumed no one else needed it and withheld praise she genuinely believed.
The fix was simply asking five questions about how the employee preferred to be led, then believing the answers.
The employee needed scheduled time, alignment before execution and room to think before committing to a view.
She warns that teams built from people like the leader share the leader's blind spots and never challenge their conclusions.
quotes: Then she told me, straight out, that she had no idea whether she was doing a good job.
I was not good at my job. I was managing a copy of myself, which takes no skill at all. The ease was not a sign I was leading well. It was a sign we were alike.
I had taken the one thing that happened to be true of me and quietly assumed it was true of everyone.
She was not harder to lead. She was harder for me to lead, which is an entirely different thing, and closing that gap was my job, not hers.

Five plain questions. I had spent years believing that reading people was an intuitive gift you either had or you did not, when most of it was simply the willingness to ask people how they worked and then believe them when they told you.
A team made in your own image is blind to the exact ground you are blind to. It will never question the instinct you should have questioned.
The people who are like you make you feel like a leader. The people who are not are the only ones who will make you into one.
